# Block 2: Inline completions {.unnumbered} Inline completion is the most familiar AI coding feature: grey "ghost text" appears as you type, suggesting a continuation. You accept with Tab, reject with Esc, or ignore it by carrying on typing. This block teaches what context inline completion uses, and the practical consequence: what you write immediately before the cursor matters more than anything else. Claude Code does not offer inline completion, so this is the one block where GitHub Copilot is the main tool. *⏱ ~25 minutes* ## Setup Use **one** completion provider at a time during this block, so you know which tool produced each suggestion. - **RStudio:** enable GitHub Copilot in RStudio's options and sign in to GitHub. - **Positron:** see Positron's completions documentation for how to choose GitHub Copilot as the provider. - **VS Code:** Copilot's AI features are built in. Select **Use AI Features** from the Copilot icon in the Status Bar and sign in with GitHub. Check it works: open a blank R script and type `# Calculate the mean of 1 to 100`. Within a second or two you should see ghost text such as `mean(1:100)`. If nothing appears, press Enter to move to the next line and wait. Copilot Free allows a limited number of completions per month (2,000 at the time of writing); paid Copilot plans do not meter completions. Completions send the code around your cursor to the provider, so the disclosure points in the [context-and-disclosure block](11d-context-disclosure-autonomy.qmd) apply here too. :::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Using Posit Assistant In RStudio and Positron you can use Posit AI Next Edit Suggestions instead of Copilot. In RStudio, turn it on from the Posit Assistant toolbar button; it requires a Posit AI account. In Positron, choose it as the completions provider. Posit AI does not meter completions. ::: ## The context principle GitHub Copilot works mainly from the current file: the code above and below the cursor, and especially the comment immediately before it. In Positron and VS Code it may also draw on other open tabs. It does not see your R session. The practical consequence: the comment immediately before your cursor, and the code above it, have the largest effect on what you get. :::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Using Posit Assistant Posit AI Next Edit Suggestions also sees your live R session: the columns of loaded data frames, functions you have defined and packages you have loaded. A session-aware provider therefore adds one more lever: what you have loaded. ::: ## Activity: The context demonstration :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} The context demonstration (10 minutes) :::: ::::{.task-container} You will use `voles_metabolism.csv`, a small synthetic dataset chosen because its column names are unlikely to appear in any model's training data. The columns are `subject_id`, `sex`, `treatment_arm`, `mass_pre_g`, `mass_post_g` and `metabolic_rate_post`. The data record a hypothetical metabolism trial in 72 voles, with three treatment arms and two sexes. **1. No context.** Restart R so that nothing is loaded. Open a blank R script, type only this comment, and wait: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # calculate the mean change in mass by treatment ``` ::: Record the suggestion. With no `library()` call, no data and no column names visible, the model has to guess. Expect something syntactically plausible but wrong for this dataset. **2. Context in the file.** Start a new blank script and add: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # Voles metabolism trial: effect of treatment on body mass # 72 voles, three treatment arms (Control, Low_dose, High_dose), two sexes # Native pipe |>, tidyverse library(tidyverse) voles <- read_csv(here::here("data", "raw", "voles_metabolism.csv")) glimpse(voles) ``` ::: Then add the same comment as before on a new line: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # calculate the mean change in mass by treatment ``` ::: Record the suggestion. A typical good result:
::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} voles |> mutate(mass_change_g = mass_post_g - mass_pre_g) |> summarise( mean_change = mean(mass_change_g, na.rm = TRUE), .by = treatment_arm ) ``` :::
The exact form varies between people and sessions; that variation is itself part of the lesson. How different were the two outputs? Did the second use column names that exist in the data? Did the model compute the change in the right direction (post minus pre)? :::: ::: :::{.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Using Posit Assistant **3. Context in the session.** With Posit AI Next Edit Suggestions, run the lines from step 2 so that `voles` exists in your session. Then open a **new, blank** script, type only the comment from step 1, and wait. If the suggestion now uses the real column names, it came from your session, not from the file. ::: ## Activity: Build a small analysis :::{.task} ::::{.task-header} Build a small analysis (10 minutes) :::: ::::{.task-container} In the script from step 2, drive inline completion through two analysis steps. Write the comment for each step first, then accept, reject or modify the suggestion. **1.** Produce a summary table of the mean and standard deviation of `mass_change_g` by `treatment_arm` and `sex`, with the number of observations per cell. (Create `mass_change_g` first if your script does not have it.) **2.** Produce one plot relating `mass_change_g` to `metabolic_rate_post`, coloured by `treatment_arm`. For each step, record the comment you wrote, the suggested code, and one line saying whether you accepted, modified or rejected it. The point of the record is to make you notice when you accepted something without inspecting it. :::: ::: :::{.callout-note} ## Check · Reproduce · Record - **Check:** accept, modify or reject every suggestion deliberately; your record of each decision is what makes you notice an unexamined acceptance. - **Reproduce:** a suggestion that names your columns correctly came from context in the file or session, so the same comment in a blank script will not reproduce it. - **Record:** nothing to log yet; the AI-use log starts in Block 4, once an agent starts doing work. ::: ## Check your understanding **The single most reliable way to improve inline suggestions in a new script is to:**

## Going further (not covered live) This material is not covered in the live session. Work through it afterwards if it is useful to you. ### The full four-step analysis The live activity uses two of four steps. The full sequence, again writing the comment for each step before accepting, rejecting or modifying the suggestion: 1. Filter to subjects with non-missing `metabolic_rate_post` and create a derived variable `mass_change_g`. 2. Produce a summary table of the mean and standard deviation of `mass_change_g` by `treatment_arm` and `sex`, with the number of observations per cell. 3. Fit a linear model of `metabolic_rate_post` on `treatment_arm` and `sex`. Inspect the coefficients. 4. Produce one plot relating `mass_change_g` to `metabolic_rate_post`, coloured by `treatment_arm`. If you can, work in pairs. Each partner attempts steps 2 and 4 independently before comparing. Comparison usually surfaces different suggestions, different acceptance decisions and, often, different bugs.
